facts.raw_span: A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting
He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness
no visual change or speech disturbance
pulse was 88 bpm
blood pressure 124/87 mmHg
oxygen saturation 98% on room air
Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb
Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus
Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology
incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma
Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation
A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made

concepts.why: The patient presented with acute right-sided weakness and vomiting, and brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla.
A 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma was found on noncontrast CT of the head.

The patient had no apparent risk factors for stroke, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.

rationales.F01: Acute right-sided weakness and vomiting suggest a stroke.
rationales.F07: Motor strength deficits are consistent with a medullary infarction.
rationales.F08: Brisk reflexes and ankle clonus suggest an upper motor neuron lesion.
rationales.F10: The incidental cavernoma could be a cause of the patient's symptoms, but it is not definitive.
rationales.F11: The recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla supports the diagnosis of medullary infarction.
rationales.F12: The diagnosis of ischemic stroke is supported by the patient's symptoms and imaging findings.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with acute right-sided weakness, numbness, and recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla on brain MRI supports medullary infarction as the most specific diagnosis.
